prompt: Some people think that all university students should study whatever they like. Others believe that they should only be allowed to study subjects that will be useful in the future, such as those related to science and technology. Discuss both these points and give your opinion.
essay:
While some people argue that all university students should be free to choose any subject they wish to study, others think that students' choices should be restricted to fields that are likely to be useful in the future, particularly in science and technology. These subjects can improve graduates' employment prospects and contribute to economic development. However, I believe that students should ultimately be allowed to select disciplines that match their abilities and interests. This essay will discuss both views and explain why freedom of choice should remain the main priority.

On the one hand, fields of study that are currently in high demand can play an important role in meeting future workforce needs. In other words, encouraging students to study subjects such as engineering, computer science and medicine can help address shortages of qualified professionals. For example, societies' increasing dependence on digital technology has created a growing need for more software developers, cybersecurity specialists and data scientists. Therefore, producing graduates in these areas can alleviate this workforce deficit, support technological progress, strengthen the economy and improve essential public services.

On the other hand, allowing students to choose subjects that correspond to their interests and abilities can increase their motivation, academic performance and long-term career satisfaction. Students are more likely to attend classes regularly, complete assignments and develop expertise when they are genuinely interested in their chosen field. By contrast, forcing them to pursue scientific or technical subjects for which they have little interest or aptitude may lead to poor results or even university dropout. For example, a student with exceptional artistic ability may build a successful career in design, architecture or the creative industries, whereas studying computer science unwillingly may prevent that individual from fulfilling their potential. Therefore, although employment prospects should be considered, students should retain the freedom to choose their own academic disciplines.

In conclusion, prioritising subjects that meet future workforce demands can benefit both graduates and the wider economy. Nevertheless, I believe that university students should ultimately be free to study disciplines that suit their interests and abilities, as personal motivation is essential for academic achievement and professional success.
